extracted.intended_audience: creative writers seeking to render authentic Yankee/regional dialect and voice (19th-century-style poetry/fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing regionally-inflected verse and prose in a Yankee dialect voice, including pronunciation representation, persona use, tone (avoidance of vulgar slang), and supplementary devices (glossary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialect as a literary advantage ('getting out of the beaten track')
rubrics_metrics.description: Beside the advantage of getting out of the beaten track, our dialect offered others hardly inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialect to achieve distinctiveness and local color rather than mere novelty. The author invokes Goethe's praise of 'behagliche naive Sprache' (comfortable naive language) that supplies 'several sensually-significant and well-sounding words ... of one, two letters, Abbreviationen, Contractionen, many short, light Sylben, new Reime' — these elements, when combined by happy constructions and lively forms, create a style with great advantages over standard literary language. Aim to exploit short words, contractions, fresh rhymes, and lively constructions to form a cohesive stylized voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation representation and typesetting ('a word more on pronunciation')
rubrics_metrics.description: A word more on pronunciation. I have endeavored to express this so far as I could by the types, taking such pains as, I fear, may sometimes make the reading harder than need be. At the same time, by studying uniformity I have sometimes been obliged to sacrifice minute exactness. The emphasis often modifies the habitual sound. For example, _for_ is commonly _fer_ (a shorter sound than _fur_ for _far_), but when emphatic it always becomes _for_, as 'wut _for!_' ... _With_ becomes sometimes _'ith_, _'ŭth_, or _'th_, or even disappears wholly where it comes before _the_, as, 'I went along _th'_ Square' ... _Without_ becomes _athout_ and _'thout_ ... _Afterwards_ always retains its locative _s_, and is pronounced always _ahterwurds'_, with a strong accent on the last syllable. ... _U_ changes in many words to _e_, always in _such, brush, tush, hush, rush, blush_, seldom in _much_ ... _T_ and _d_, _b_ and _p_, _v_ and _w_, remain intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent pronunciation consistently but not slavishly: favor uniform conventions even if they sacrifice minute exactness. Use typesetting (phonetic respellings, apostrophes) to indicate habitual sounds and emphatic shifts. Give explicit examples for common changes (for→fer; too/to; to→ta, toe; with→'ith/'th or elision; without→athout/'thout; u→e in certain words). Note that emphasis can alter expected pronunciations; mark emphatic forms when needed. Avoid inventing ad hoc respellings that confuse the reader—consistency aids comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate provincialisms from slang; avoid affected vulgarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Of course in what I have said I wish to be understood as keeping in mind the difference between provincialisms properly so called and _slang_. _Slang_ is always vulgar, because it is not a natural but an affected way of talking, and all mere tricks of speech or writing are offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing regional speech, use authentic provincialisms rather than artificial slang. Authentic regionalisms arise naturally from lived speech and can carry dignity or refinement; affected slang reads vulgar and undermines the work. Refrain from 'mere tricks of speech or writing'—prioritize truthful, organic voice over gimmicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the persona's voice when writing under an assumed character
rubrics_metrics.description: Now, in the first place, I was writing under an assumed character, and must talk as the person would whose mouthpiece I made myself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a pseudonymous or fictional speaker, render speech and thought as that character would genuinely produce them. Defend utterances as in-character rather than authorial statements. Fidelity to the persona's vocabulary, attitudes, and idioms is necessary for credibility (even when those expressions might be objectionable if attributed to the author).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity through lived experience and study of local speech
rubrics_metrics.description: To me the dialect was native, was spoken all about me when a boy ... Since then I have made a study of it so far as opportunity allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground dialect writing in firsthand familiarity or careful study of local speech. Observe real speakers (or historical records) rather than relying on secondhand caricature. Such study improves accuracy of pronunciation, idiom, and register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow refined sentiment alongside comic or shrewd elements
rubrics_metrics.description: I should have entirely failed in my design, if I had not made it appear that high and even refined sentiment may coexist with the shrewder and more comic elements of the Yankee character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce regional or comic characters to flat comic foils; mix heartfelt or elevated sentiment with humor and shrewdness to create fuller, more humane portrayals. Balancing tones can prevent caricature and broaden appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity in prefatory material ('prefaces should be')
rubrics_metrics.description: But life is short, and prefaces should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep prefaces and introductory remarks concise. Use them to explain essential matters (tone, persona, scope, pronunciation conventions, authenticity claims) but avoid lengthy digressions that distract from the work itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a glossary/index to aid readers
rubrics_metrics.description: II. GLOSSARY TO THE BIGLOW PAPERS
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantial dialectal vocabulary or archaisms are used, supply a glossary or explanatory index for readers unfamiliar with terms (definitions, variant spellings, and notes on usage). This preserves authenticity while ensuring accessibility.
